definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The imperishable person (akṣara puruṣa), called kūṭastha, set beside the perishable, which is all beings; the highest person, the Lord, is higher even than it (15.16-15.18).

name: The inverted aśvattha tree of saṃsāra

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 15.1–5: 'they speak of' an imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, its leaves the metres; knowing it one knows the Veda; its branches spread below and above, swollen by the guṇas, with sense-objects as shoots, and its roots below are bound up with action in the human world; its form, end, beginning and foundation are not perceived here; having cut it with the strong weapon of non-attachment one is to seek the place of no return, taking refuge in the primal person from whom the ancient activity flowed; the undeluded, free of pride, delusion, attachment and desire, reach that imperishable place. (The verses do not themselves name the tree saṃsāra.)

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: unswerving devotion to Kṛṣṇa by a yoga with no other is counted among the dispositions called knowledge (13.11); his devotee, knowing field, knowledge and knowable, becomes fit for his state (13.19); one who serves him with the unswerving yoga of devotion goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); one who knows him as puruṣottama worships him with his whole being (15.19).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The roots of the aśvattha stretch below in the human world, binding through action (karma-anubandhin) (15.2); rajas binds the embodied one by attachment to action (14.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, neither sat nor asat (13.13); it has hands, feet, eyes and ears everywhere and stands enveloping all (13.14); appears through the sense-qualities yet is without senses, is unattached yet supports all, without guṇas yet their experiencer (13.15); is inside and outside beings, moving and unmoving, not to be known through subtlety, far and near (13.16); undivided yet as if divided, sustainer, devourer and generator of beings (13.17); light of lights beyond darkness, knowledge, knowable and reached by knowledge, set in the heart of all (13.18); seeing the many as resting in the one one attains brahman (13.31); by unswerving devotion one becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); Kṛṣṇa is the foundation of brahman (14.27).

name: The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: puruṣa, situated in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of prakṛti, and attachment to them causes its births in good and bad wombs (13.22); whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, is from the union (saṃyoga) of the field and the knower of the field (13.27).

name: Dying while a guṇa predominates (BhG 14.14–15, 14.18)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The guṇa that has increased when the embodied one dies decides what follows: dying when sattva has increased, it reaches the stainless worlds of those who know the highest (14.14); dying in rajas it is born among those attached to action, and dissolved in tamas in deluded wombs (14.15). Those abiding in sattva go upward, the rājasa stay in the middle, and the tāmasa, abiding in the workings of the lowest guṇa, go downward (14.18). The fruits of the guṇas are named in 14.16: the stainless fruit of well-done action, pain, ignorance.

notes: Merged from extractor A's cpt:dying-in-a-predominant-guna and extractor B's cpt:gunas-and-destiny-after-death (both new). The verse's 'pralayaṃ yāti' is dying, the same word as the cosmic dissolution of 14.2. Compare cpt:last-thought-at-death (8.5-6), which concerns the last thought, not the prevailing guṇa.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Constant evenness of thought (sama-cittatva) when the wanted or unwanted befalls is among the dispositions called knowledge (13.10); one who sees the supreme lord standing the same (samam) in all beings sees, and seeing him equally present everywhere does not harm himself and goes to the highest goal (13.28–29); the one gone beyond the guṇas is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, the pleasant and the unpleasant, blame and praise, honour and dishonour, friend and foe (14.24–25).

name: The paths of the Gītā: action, knowledge, meditation and devotion

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Some see the self in themselves by themselves through meditation, others by the yoga of sāṃkhya, others by the yoga of action (13.25); others, not knowing thus, worship after hearing from others and they too cross death (13.26); unswerving bhakti-yoga carries one beyond the guṇas (14.26). The verses set these side by side without ranking them.

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the teaching on field and knower has been sung by the seers, in the metres and in the brahmasūtra words (13.5); attendance on the teacher is among the dispositions called knowledge (13.8); some worship having heard from others (13.26); the knowledge of the guṇas is announced as the highest, by which all the sages reached perfection (14.1); chapter 15 is called 'this most secret teaching' (15.20).

name: The guṇas as the doers of action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The seer who sees no doer other than the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains the Lord's state (14.19); the one beyond the guṇas stands firm, knowing only that 'the guṇas are operating' (14.23). Actions are done by prakṛti alone (13.30).

name: Going beyond the guṇas (guṇātīta)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Having gone beyond the three guṇas, from which the body arises, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age and pain, attains immortality (14.20). Asked for the marks, the conduct and the means (14.21), Kṛṣṇa describes one who neither hates illumination, activity and delusion when present nor longs for them when gone; who sits as one indifferent, unshaken, knowing only that 'the guṇas are operating'; who is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, in blame and praise, honour and dishonour, toward friend and foe, and has given up all undertakings (14.22-14.25). The means named is serving the Lord with unswerving bhakti-yoga, by which one goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); seeing no doer but the guṇas and knowing what is beyond them leads to the Lord's state (14.19).

relations.note: the state of one no longer bound by the guṇas (14.5, 14.20)

notes: New concept (extractor B) for the Gītā's portrait of the one gone beyond the guṇas, the counterpart of cpt:sthitaprajna (2.54–72) and cpt:qualities-of-the-devotee (12.13–20); extractor A records it through trm:gunatita and phn:marks-of-gunatita. The text does not call this state liberation while living; compare cpt:liberation-while-living (U05), whose Gītā definition names 'the one beyond the guṇas'.

name: The eternal, unslayable embodied one (dehin / śarīrin)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 14.5: the guṇas bind the imperishable embodied one (dehinam avyayam) in the body; 14.20: the embodied one who goes beyond them attains the immortal.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's eternal portion 'having become the living being' (jīva-bhūta) in the world of the living draws the senses with the mind as sixth (15.7); as master (īśvara) of the body it takes them with it when it obtains a body and when it departs from one, as the wind carries scents from their seat (15.8); presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, smell and the mind it partakes of objects (15.9). The deluded do not see it departing, staying or enjoying, accompanied by the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see it, and striving yogins see it established in themselves (15.10–11).

name: The soul as a part (aṃśa) of Brahman

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'A portion (aṃśa) of me indeed, eternal, having become the living being (jīva-bhūta) in the world of the living' draws to itself the senses with the mind as the sixth, which abide in prakṛti (15.7). The verse says 'of me' (the speaker, Kṛṣṇa), not 'of brahman'; the commentators divide on the sense of 'portion' (an apparent part, a real part as mode, a separated part; dsp:bhagavad-gita-jiva-as-amsa).

notes: Chs. 13–15 contribution, from extractor A's entry (cpt:jiva-as-part-of-brahman) and extractor B's new cpt:jiva-as-amsa (mapped here: reuse of the data/ id). B's account of the living being's activity in 15.8–11 is recorded under cpt:jiva.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the fruit of well-done action (karmaṇaḥ sukṛtasya) is said to be sāttvika and stainless, the fruit of rajas pain, the fruit of tamas ignorance (14.16); rajas binds by attachment to action (14.7); actions are done in every way by prakṛti alone (13.30).

name: The field and the knower of the field (kṣetra–kṣetrajña)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: This body is called the field and whoever knows it the knower of the field (13.2); the Lord is to be known as the knower of the field in all fields, and knowledge of field and knower is knowledge (13.3). The field in brief: the great elements, the sense of 'I', understanding, the unmanifest, the ten faculties and the one, the five domains of the senses, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience and steadiness, with their modifications (13.6-13.7). Every being arises from the union of field and knower (13.27); the possessor of the field illumines the whole field as the sun the world (13.34); those who know their difference with the eye of knowledge go to the highest (13.35).

members: ekam ('the one'; manas per the commentators)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The chapters name the goal as: not being born again (13.24); crossing beyond death (13.26); going to the highest goal (13.29) or to the supreme (13.35), with release from the prakṛti of beings (13.35); reaching brahman (13.31); the highest perfection (14.1) and, having come to the same nature as the Lord, not being born at creation nor troubled at dissolution (14.2); the immortal, freedom from birth, death, old age and pain (13.13, 14.20); fitness for becoming brahman (14.26); the place from which none return, the Lord's supreme abode (15.4–6). Whether 'my state' (mad-bhāva, 13.19, 14.19) names the same goal the commentators read differently.

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Kṛṣṇa says he is seated in the heart of all, and that memory, knowledge and removal (apohana: their loss, or the removal of doubt) come from him (15.15); the knowable is said to be set in the heart of all (13.18).

name: Great brahman as the Lord's womb; the Lord as seed-giving father (BhG 14.3–4)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord's womb is great brahman (mahad brahma); in it he places the germ, and from that the origin of all beings comes (14.3). Of whatever forms come into being in all wombs, great brahman is the womb and the Lord is the seed-giving father (14.4). The commentators take 'great brahman' here as prakṛti; the verses call it only 'great brahman' and 'my womb'.

notes: New concept, merged from extractor A's cpt:mahad-brahma-as-womb and extractor B's cpt:mahad-brahma-yoni. The commentators identify this 'great brahman' with prakṛti (the Lord's prakṛti of the three guṇas, or non-conscious matter in its subtle state); the verses do not use that word. Compare 9.10 (prakṛti gives birth under the Lord's oversight) and 7.10 (the Lord as the eternal seed of all beings).

name: The self is not the agent; the guṇas act

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: prakṛti is the cause in agency (13.21); one who sees actions done by prakṛti alone and his self as not the doer sees (13.30); the supreme self, beginningless and without guṇas, though in the body neither acts nor is tainted (13.32), as space is not tainted (13.33); the seer who beholds no agent other than the guṇas attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20); it is the cause in agency concerning effect and cause (13.21); puruṣa abides in it and experiences the guṇas born of it (13.22); all actions are done by prakṛti alone (13.30); the three guṇas are born of it (14.5); the senses and mind abide in it (15.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Beginningless like prakṛti (13.20), puruṣa is the cause in experiencing pleasure and pain (13.21); abiding in prakṛti it experiences the guṇas, and attachment to them is the cause of its births in good and bad wombs (13.22). The highest person in this body is onlooker, consenter, sustainer, experiencer, great lord, and is called the supreme self (13.23); whoever knows puruṣa and prakṛti with the guṇas thus is not born again (13.24). Chapter 15 speaks of two persons, perishable and imperishable, and the highest person beyond both (15.16-15.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: attachment to the guṇas causes puruṣa's births in good and bad wombs (13.22); one who knows puruṣa and prakṛti is not born again (13.24); dying in sattva, rajas or tamas leads to the stainless worlds, to birth among those attached to action, or to deluded wombs (14.14–15, 14.18); the living being takes the senses and mind with it from body to body as the wind carries scents (15.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 13.23: the highest puruṣa in this body is called the onlooker (upadraṣṭṛ), with consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord and supreme self. (The Gītā's word here is upadraṣṭṛ, not sākṣin.)

Bhagavad Gītā 15.4: after cutting the aśvattha, the place of no return is to be sought with the words 'I take refuge (prapadye) in that very primal person from whom the ancient activity flowed forth'.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Some see the self in themselves by themselves through meditation (13.25); whoever sees oneself as not the doer sees truly (13.30); the supreme self neither acts nor is stained though in the body (13.32), and the self present in the body is unstained like space (13.33); striving yogins see the one abiding in themselves (15.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Sattva, rajas and tamas arise from prakṛti and bind the imperishable embodied one in the body (14.5): sattva, stainless, illuminating and free of affliction, binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge; rajas, of the nature of passion, by attachment to action; tamas, born of ignorance and deluding, by heedlessness, idleness and sleep (14.6–9). Each prevails by overpowering the other two (14.10). Signs: illumination — knowledge — at all the gates of the body (sattva); greed, activity, undertaking, restlessness, craving (rajas); absence of illumination, inactivity, heedlessness, delusion (tamas) (14.11–13). Dying in each leads to the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest, to birth among those attached to action, or to deluded wombs (14.14–15); their fruits are the stainless, pain and ignorance (14.16); from them come knowledge, greed, and heedlessness, delusion and ignorance (14.17); those abiding in them go upward, stay in the middle, go downward (14.18). One who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is higher than them attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19); going beyond them one attains the immortal (14.20; marks 14.22–25; means 14.26). In chapters 13 and 15: the modifications and the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20); attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22); the branches of the aśvattha are swollen by the guṇas (15.2).

name: The perishable, the imperishable and the highest person

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: There are two persons in the world, the perishable — all beings — and the imperishable, called the one standing firm (kūṭastha) (15.16); the highest person is another, called the supreme self, the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds (15.17); since the Lord is beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable he is celebrated as puruṣottama (15.18); whoever knows him thus worships him with his whole being (15.19). The commentators divide on what the imperishable is.

notes: Chs. 13–15 contribution, merged from extractor B's cpt:three-purusas and extractor A's cpt:ksara-aksara-purusottama (the Dvaita unit's concept for the same verses, flagged for S5). What the akṣara denotes is read differently by the commentators (dsp:bhagavad-gita-aksara-purusa).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13.6–7: the field is listed as the great elements, ahaṅkāra, buddhi, the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one, the five ranges of the senses, with desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience and steadiness; the text does not number them.

name: The virtues called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 13.8–12 (vulgate 13.7–11): twenty dispositions are declared 'knowledge' (jñāna), and what is other than them 'ignorance'. The verse lists them without further grouping.

members: indriyārtheṣu vairāgya (dispassion toward the objects of the senses)
janma-mṛtyu-jarā-vyādhi-duḥkha-doṣānudarśana (keeping in view the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness and pain)
anabhiṣvaṅga toward son, wife, home and the like (absence of clinging)
nityaṃ sama-cittatvam iṣṭāniṣṭopapattiṣu (constant evenness of thought when the wanted or unwanted befalls)
mayi ananya-yogena bhaktir avyabhicāriṇī (unswerving devotion to the Lord through a yoga with no other)
aratir jana-saṃsadi (no delight in gatherings of people)
adhyātma-jñāna-nityatva (constancy in the knowledge of what pertains to the self)
tattva-jñānārtha-darśana (keeping in view the aim of the knowledge of reality)
notes: The count of twenty depends on counting asakti and anabhiṣvaṅga separately and the two items of 13.12 separately; the text itself gives no number. This edition numbers the verses 13.8–12.

name: The self common to all men (vaiśvānara)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 15.14: Kṛṣṇa, becoming Vaiśvānara and dwelling in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, digests the fourfold food.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the radiance in the sun, the moon and fire is the Lord's (15.12); entering the earth he sustains beings by his vigour and, becoming soma, nourishes all plants (15.13); becoming vaiśvānara in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna, he digests the fourfold food (15.14). The word vibhūti is not used here; the verses continue the manner of 7.8–11 and 10.19–42.
